CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Bruce Ward is a 52-year-old male seen in consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for possible surgical intervention for a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion. Mr. Ward presented to Dr. Howard on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denied any trouble with headaches in the past. Workup for worsening headaches was initiated with a brain MRI and serology, where a pituitary lesion was incidentally discovered. 

He reports that his headaches started about three months ago and have been getting worse over time. At first, the severity was about a three out of 10, and it gradually worsened to about six out of 10 severity. The headaches are located behind his eyes, described as a dull nagging ache, and tend to be worse in the morning. They last a few hours at a time, and nothing makes them better or worse. He tried Tylenol a few times for the headaches, but it did not work, so he stopped. 

He denies feeling sick, fevers, rashes, neck issues, numbness, tingling, or ever passing out. He notes that recently he seems to be bumping into door frames, though he did not notice any change in his vision or balance, and his eyes were checked in the fall.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
• General: Denies feeling sick or fevers.
• Skin: Denies rashes.
• Neurological: Endorses worsening headaches. Denies numbness or tingling. Endorses bumping into door frames.
• Neck: Denies neck issues or stiffness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable.

SURGICAL HISTORY
None.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years and recently bought a small house. Denies use of alcohol, tobacco, or recreational drugs. Adopted, family history unknown.

FAMILY HISTORY
Adopted, so family history is unknown.

MEDICATIONS
None currently. Tried Tylenol a few times without relief.

ALLERGIES
None noted.

VITALS
Not documented.

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Appropriate affect and fluent speech.
Cranial Nerves: Grossly intact.
Motor/Sensory: No focal, motor, or sensory deficit in the upper or lower extremities.
Eyes: Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21 (personally reviewed): CBC, U&Es, coagulation, and CRP were all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates a low TSH; all other results were normal.
Radiology from 3/4/21 (personally reviewed): Brain MRI with contrast reveals a pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size, and no other abnormalities are noted.

ASSESSMENT
Pituitary adenoma. Mr. Ward is a 52-year-old male with a benign-appearing pituitary adenoma incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. He is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression, therefore surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated.

PLAN
• Surgical intervention: Surgical intervention via a transsphenoidal approach is indicated to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa due to vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm. Discussed risks of anesthesia (including heart attack, stroke, death) and risks of surgery (including infection, need for further surgery, spinal fluid leak or infection requiring prolonged hospitalization or additional procedure, seizure, stroke, permanent numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking, or death). The patient will see surgery scheduler Deborah to set up the surgery.
• Ophthalmology referral: Referral to an eye doctor for a full exam and a visual field test to map peripheral vision prior to surgery and monitor after surgery.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

She tolerated it for four days before going to the emergency room because nothing she did relieved it. The ER ran an EKG and did blood tests, and everything was normal. 

The pain was located in the center of her chest, right behind her breastbone, and felt really sharp, like she was having a heart attack. She does not recall waking up with it, and it happened randomly. The pain was worse with eating, and she also experienced difficulty swallowing. Both the chest pain and swallowing problem got better about three days after she went to the ER. She does not think she has ever had heartburn, so she is not sure what that feels like. She has been trying to lose weight. She notes she was going through a really stressful job transition right around the time this happened. She denies any abdominal pain and reports her bowel movements are normal.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
• Cardiovascular: Had a four-day episode of sharp central chest pain behind the breastbone in October 2020, which has since resolved. Normal cardiac workup in the ER including EKG and blood tests.
• Gastrointestinal: Endorsed difficulty swallowing during the episode of chest pain. Denies heartburn (unsure what it feels like). Pain was worse with eating. Denies abdominal pain. Bowel movements are normal.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Uterine fibroids, anemia.

SURGICAL HISTORY
Gallbladder removal several years ago.

FAMILY HISTORY
No known family history of GI problems.

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Appears well.
Abdomen: Mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants. No pain or tenderness with push on lower belly. Otherwise, examination looks normal and good.

RESULTS
ER records reviewed, including normal cardiac workup, EKG, and blood tests.

ASSESSMENT
Betty Hill is a new patient with a history of uterine fibroids and anemia presenting with a past episode of chest pain and difficulty swallowing from October 2020 that has since resolved. Possible etiologies include GERD, dyspepsia, esophagitis, musculoskeletal etiologies, and anxiety. Suspect she had an anxiety attack related to her job transition, plus or minus a contribution from her musculoskeletal etiologies.

PLAN
We discussed doing an EGD or upper endoscopy versus monitoring for symptoms. The patient elected to hold off on the EGD and self-monitor her symptoms, as she has been asymptomatic for three months and likely any esophagitis would already be healed. 

INSTRUCTIONS
Call the office if you have any additional episodes of pain or any other symptoms you're concerned about, at which point we will get you scheduled for an EGD. Otherwise, follow up as needed for any other GI complaints.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Kidney evaluation in the setting of Smith-Magenis syndrome.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Katherine is a 22-month-old former twin born at 34 and 3/8 weeks who presents for a kidney evaluation. She has a history of Smith-Magenis syndrome diagnosed by a neurologist. When the twins were born, Katherine weighed 4 pounds 8 ounces, and her twin was 3 pounds 13 ounces. Katherine had early problems with eating where she would stop breathing when eating, and a hard time regulating her temperature. She has a GI doctor for severe reflux and a dietician who recommended taking her off cow's milk (she now drinks Ripple pea protein milk, water, and water with a little juice). She has seen an allergist, a neurologist, an orthopedic specialist, an ophthalmologist, an audiologist, and a geneticist. The geneticist noted that individuals with this syndrome can have trouble with their kidneys, such as kidneys fusing into one, and problems with their legs. 

Regarding her developmental milestones, she was not walking or sitting by herself at one year old. Currently, she is crawling and trying to take steps. She is involved in multiple therapies including feeding therapy, occupational therapy, physical therapy, and speech therapy starting within the next couple of weeks. 

Her twin sister is running around with no problems, is about the same size (they wear the same clothes), and is a little taller. Katherine is slightly shorter and chunkier. 

Review of fluid intake and output reveals she has around 8 to 10 wet diapers in a 24-hour period, drinks a lot, and urinates frequently.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
• Gastrointestinal: History of severe reflux.
• Neurological: History of delayed motor milestones (not walking or sitting by one year old, currently crawling and trying to take steps). History of hypotonia.
• Constitutional: Drinks a lot and urinates frequently (8 to 10 wet diapers per day).

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
• Smith-Magenis syndrome
• Prematurity (born at 34 and 3/8 weeks as a twin)
• Severe gastroesophageal reflux

FAMILY HISTORY
• Sibling: Nine-year-old brother with autism. Twin sister who is developing typically.
• Family history of kidney failure, dialysis, or transplant: None.

SOCIAL HISTORY
• The patient lives in Dallas, Georgia.

PHYSICAL EXAM
• General: Well-nourished female, slightly fussy when examined.
• Eyes: Small appearing.
• Cardiovascular: Normal heart sounds.
• Respiratory: Normal breath sounds.
• Ears: Examined without acute findings.
• Extremities/Neuromuscular: Mild hypotonia of the lower extremities and in her arms.
• Genitourinary: Normal external female genitalia.

RESULTS
• Kidney ultrasound ordered to screen for congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Katherine is a 22-month-old former 34 and 3/8-week-old twin with Smith-Magenis syndrome. Several organ systems can be affected by this chromosomal deletion syndrome. Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract have been reported in the literature.

We will obtain a screening of the kidneys by ultrasound today downstairs. If there are abnormalities on the kidney ultrasound, we will determine next steps and future follow-up. 

INSTRUCTIONS
• Complete the kidney ultrasound today downstairs.
• If the ultrasound is normal, no further follow-up with nephrology is needed. If it is abnormal, follow-up will be scheduled at the Kennesaw (Town Center) location.
• The nurse will come in to have you complete paperwork and provide instructions for the ultrasound.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right wrist injury after a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Diana is a female presenting with severe right wrist pain following an injury that occurred yesterday morning. The patient reports she was doing laundry, carrying a basket, and a clothes basket caused a shirt to fall out. She was trying to catch it, missed a step on the stairs, slipped, and put her arms out to catch herself. She landed and her right wrist started to hurt very badly and became swollen. She rates the pain as a 9 out of 10. To ease the pain, she applied ice, used an ace wrap at home, and took some ibuprofen, which helped a little bit. The pain is located along her wrist and does not extend elsewhere, though she notes a little bit of tingling in her fingers, which she cannot tell if it is due to the swelling. She denies prior injury to this arm.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
• Constitutional: Denies fever.
• Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain or palpitations.
• Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
• Neurological: Endorses a little bit of tingling in the fingers of the right hand.
• Musculoskeletal: Endorses severe right wrist pain, swelling, and difficulty moving the wrist in any direction. Denies prior right arm injury.

VITALS
• Blood Pressure: 140/70
• Heart Rate: 80 beats per minute
• Temperature: 97.2 degrees
• Respiratory Rate: 20 breaths per minute

PHYSICAL EXAM
• Head and Neck: No adenopathy, no thyromegaly, no carotid bruit.
• Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur, no rub, no gallop.
• Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
• Lower Extremities: Palpable pulses, no lower edema.
• Upper Extremities / Right Wrist Examination: Normal range of motion of shoulders and upper extremities otherwise. Right wrist shows obvious swelling and bruising (ecchymosis). Tenderness on palpation throughout. Pain on flexion, extension, radial deviation, and lateral (adduction/abduction) movement. Unable to make a tight fist. Evidence of potential fracture with bony crepitus felt.

RESULTS
• X-ray: Positive for a Colles' fracture of the right wrist. The fracture appears extra-articular and usually proximal to the radial ulnar joint. Dorsal angulation of the distal fracture fragment is present to a variable degree. Ulnar styloid fracture is present.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
• Primary Diagnosis: Colles' fracture of the right wrist (extra-articular fracture proximal to the radial ulnar joint with dorsal angulation and ulnar styloid fracture).
• Treatment Plan: 
  - Conservative/initial immobilization: Provide a brace for the arm today.
  - Surgical intervention: Recommend surgery as the best course of action to get the wrist straight and place screws to hold it in place and prevent malformation. The procedure will involve an overnight stay.
  - Medications: Prescribe Ultram 50 mg every six hours for pain.
  - Physical Therapy: Initiate physical therapy a few weeks after surgery, approximately three times a week to strengthen the wrist.
  - Bracing duration: Patient will need to wear the brace for about six weeks.
  - Follow-up / Vacation planning: Reassess at a checkup in a month to evaluate healing status and determine if her upcoming vacation in a month (lasting a couple of weeks) can proceed based on physical therapy progression.

CHIEF COMPLAINT

Abnormal lab work showing a low immunoglobulin A level.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

The patient is a male who presents for evaluation of a low immunoglobulin A (IgA) level noted on recent routine physical lab work by his PCP. The patient reports feeling anxious about the abnormal result. He states that he tends to get frequent colds in the wintertime that seem to linger, though he is unsure if this is more than usual. He denies frequent diarrhea or abdominal infections. 

He was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes by his PCP and started on metformin. He notes his family owns a donut shop at the end of the street. He denies any history of needing blood products or a blood transfusion, though he previously attempted to donate blood and did not qualify due to recent international travel to Zambia.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY

Type 2 diabetes.

SOCIAL HISTORY

Recent international travel to Zambia. Family owns a donut shop.

FAMILY HISTORY

Family is described as pretty healthy. No known family history of immune deficiencies.

VITALS

Vitals and weight collected by assistants reviewed; no fever and everything looks good.

PHYSICAL EXAM

• Cardiovascular: Nice regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs appreciated.
• Respiratory: Lungs are clear; no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
• Neck: No lymphadenopathy or swollen lymph glands.
• Abdominal: Soft; no tenderness to palpation.

RESULTS

Recent lab work is consistent with an IgA deficiency (low immunoglobulin A level).

ASSESSMENT

Immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency. This is a very common immunodeficiency where the body's IgA antibody level is lower than normal. Most people live their entire lives without knowing they have it and function perfectly. Some people may get frequent respiratory, sinus, or abdominal infections, but this does not appear to be the case for the patient. While it can go along with other immunodeficiencies, there is a low likelihood of that in his case.

PLAN

• Order additional blood work to check other antibodies.
• Patient education: Advised the patient not to worry. Instructed him to watch for infections that do not stop or are hard to get under control, or changes to the abdominal tract such as severe diarrhea.
• Precautions regarding blood products: Instructed the patient that if he ever ends up needing blood products, he must inform them that he has an IgA deficiency due to the risk of a strong bodily reaction.
• Have the patient complete the ordered lab work.

They looked and saw that the blister had become unroofed with thick, soft, mushy skin underneath, having a bad smell with some yellow drainage.

Regarding pain, it was stinging initially, but now it is throbbing like a fire poker in the bottom of his foot. The inside of his calf muscle is really hard, and every time he pushes it, he feels it all the way up to his knee behind his kneecap. Additionally, he has been coughing a lot the last two days and has had a difficult time catching his breath when walking around the house.

He has a history of diabetes and diabetic neuropathy. His A1c has been 6.7 for about two years, and he rarely has a blood sugar over 200, checking 2-3 times a day. However, his sugars have been trending in the 300s to 400s over the last two weeks, with one spike at 500 to 600.

Diabetes.
Diabetic neuropathy.

Slight fever noted. Otherwise, vitals look good.

• Vascular: Bilateral palpable femoral and popliteal pulses are present. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are not palpable, but are present via Doppler.

• Right foot X-ray: No evidence of osteomyelitis; no infection of the bone.

Nonhealing diabetic foot ulcer on the right foot.
